title: Infra GPU Fleet + Cloud Accounts / Networking / IaC / CI-CD Playbook (2026)
author: Emily Zhao
content:
Summary:
This playbook consolidates operational standards and actionable runbooks for GPU fleet capacity, cloud account structure and networking, Terraform/IaC module hygiene, and CI/CD for infra changes. It is intended for infra engineers, SRE, and platform owners responsible for procurement, scaling, and safe rollout of GPU-backed inference capacity.

Context and goals:
- Keep latency and availability predictable as capacity scales.
- Maintain clear ownership and minimal blast radius for infra changes.
- Standardize Terraform modules & CI/CD to enable safe, auditable rolls (including canary/preview).
- Provide on-call runbooks for common capacity events and networking incidents.

Contents (document map):
1) Ownership and capacity model
2) Cloud accounts and network topology
3) Terraform / IaC module standards
4) CI/CD and build pipeline for infra changes
5) GPU fleet runbooks (capacity, node failures, degraded performance)
6) Operational playbooks and escalation paths
7) Appendix: examples and checklists

1) Ownership and capacity model
- Capacity owner: infra-gpu-capacity (primary), eng-sre (secondary).
- Service-level targets:
  - 99.9% availability for serving pools tagged production during business hours (PST).
  - Median p99 tail latency for token generation pipelines <= 120ms on provisioned NVMe + A100-equivalent node; adjust per model profile.
- Buffer policy: maintain 20% spare reserved capacity for scheduled traffic and 10% for on-demand burst across pools by region.
- Capacity types:
  - Base reserved (committed monthly) for predictable traffic.
  - Burst (ephemeral) autoscaled for short peaks.
  - Spot / preemptible pools used for best-effort workloads (non-prod, training).

Capacity planning cadence:
1. Weekly demand snapshot (infra-gpu-capacity) dashboard: token/sec, concurrent sessions, queue length.
2. Monthly forecast with product (/product) teams adjust reserved commits 30-60 days ahead.
3. Pre-holiday or campaign prep: 6-week lead time.

2) Cloud accounts and network topology
- Account structure (AWS example):
  - redwood-org-root (org-level governance)
  - accounts/prod-inference-<region> (contains prod GPU fleets + NAT/GW egress controls)
  - accounts/dedicated-gpu-<customer> (VPC-isolated customer-dedicated clusters)
  - accounts/staging-inference-<region>
  - accounts/shared-networking (transit gateways, central egress, DNS)
- Networking pattern:
  - Each GPU fleet runs in a dedicated VPC per region and environment.
  - Transit Gateway connects fleet VPCs to shared services (auth, metrics, artifact stores) with explicit route tables per env.
  - Egress control: use centralized NAT/GW with egress proxy + logging for compliance customers.
  - Security groups: deny-by-default, only allow control-plane (TLS 443) from shared-management subnets and health-check ports (TCP 9000) from load balancing subnets.

Subnet layout (example):
- 3 AZs per region, each AZ: public LB subnet, private compute subnet (GPU nodes), private management subnet.

Networking operational notes:
- MTU must be consistent across ENIs and Transit Gateway (1500 recommended unless jumbo frames proven).
- EC2 placement groups: use cluster placement for low-latency multi-GPU nodes where required by model shards. Document in module if used.

3) Terraform / IaC module standards
Objective: modules are small, composable, well-documented, and enforce policy checks.
Standards checklist (must pass pre-merge):
- Module README with purpose, inputs, outputs, and example usage.
- Idempotent: apply should not make changes unless spec differs.
- Input validation using variable constraints + explicit types.
- Outputs limited to essential resources (IDs, ARNs, connection strings).
- No hard-coded credentials or secrets; consume via Vault/KMS references.
- Tagging convention: {team:infra, project:redwood-inference, env:prod, owner:infra-gpu-capacity}.
- Semantic versioning for modules (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH).
- Change process: non-breaking additions allowed in minor/patch; breaking changes require major version bump + migration guide.

Module naming and repo layout (Table-like listing):
- module/gpu-cluster creates ASG/EC2 fleet or managed node group for GPU instances
- module/network-vpc VPC, subnets, route tables, NAT/GW, VPC endpoints
- module/transit-gw Transit Gateway attachment and routes
- module/iam-role permission boundary + roles for fleet control plane
- module/monitoring metrics, log groups, alarm defaults

Policy-as-code: all terraform in the infra repo must pass terraform fmt -> tflint -> terraform validate -> terratest unit checks -> opa/policy enforcement (conftest/OPA with rego) in CI.

4) CI/CD and build pipeline for infra changes
Principles:
- All infra changes must be PR-reviewed with automated plan preview and policy checks.
- Apply to prod must be gated: approvals from infra-sre + capacity owner or scheduled window.
- Use ephemeral plan environments for review (pipelines create a plan and a human-readable plan artifact).

Pipeline stages (high-level):
1. pre-commit: terraform fmt, tflint (fast feedback).
2. CI: terraform init & validate, unit tests, terratest, conftest policy checks.
3. PR comment: show terraform plan summary and cost-estimate.
4. Integration stage (staging): optional automatic apply to staging after green tests.
5. Canaries & prod deploy: staged apply with a canary subset when changing fleet scaling, ASG settings, or network routes.

Canary strategy for scaling/network changes:
- Create a canary fleet in a single AZ with 10% of target capacity and route 1-2% of traffic for 15-30 minutes. Monitor key metrics (error rate, token latency, queue length).
- If metrics remain within thresholds, proceed to gradual rollout over remaining AZs.
- Rollback plan: terraform apply of previous version & immediate traffic shift to fallback model variant or region.

Release windows and approvals:
- Prod applies must be scheduled in the infra calendar with 2 approvers from infra-sre and infra-gpu-capacity. Emergency changes use the oncall escalation process (section 6).

5) GPU fleet runbooks (selected scenarios)
Runbook: queue growth / insufficient capacity
1. Detect: monitoring alerts when queue length > 50 requests for > 5 minutes or average wait time > 300s.
2. Initial responder: infra-gpu-capacity oncall.
3. Immediate steps:
  a. Validate health of control plane: check autoscaler logs and AWS ASG activity.
  b. Check recent CI/CD changes: link PRs that touched scaling policies in the last 60 minutes.
  c. If burstable capacity available, trigger scale-up policy (manual override) to add +20% nodes: 
     - CLI (example):
       aws autoscaling set-desired-capacity --auto-scaling-group-name rgw-prod-gpu-asg --desired-capacity 120 --region us-west-2
  d. If no burst, failover traffic to fallback region using runbook-step documented in ops-console (routing change takes ~2-5 min).
4. Post-incident: create incident ticket, link dashboards, and perform root-cause analysis within 72 hours.

Runbook: node GPU degradation (e.g., memory errors, noisy neighbor)
1. Detect: metrics show increased OOMs, CUDA errors, or degraded p99 latency for single node.
2. Quarantine node: mark instance as draining in LB/pool, cordon via orchestration (kube: kubectl cordon; autoscaling group: set instance to Standby).
3. Replace: trigger replacement through ASG or node group, tag for hardware investigation.

Runbook: networking blackhole between fleet and shared metrics/kv stores
1. Detect: missing heartbeat to control plane or metrics ingestion errors across AZs.
2. Verify route tables and Transit Gateway attachments.
3. If route propagation missing, reattach TGW or refresh VGW config. Use CloudOps playbook for cross-account route fixes.

6) Operational playbooks and escalation paths
- Oncall rotations: infra-gpu-capacity 1-week rotation. Primary oncall handles incident triage, secondary takes over if escalation needed.
- Pager rules: P0 (service unavailable) -> page primary + infra-sre lead; P1 (degraded) -> page primary.
- Escalation matrix:
  - 0-15 min: primary responder (infra-gpu-capacity)
  - 15-45 min: involve infra-sre and networking lead
  - 45+ min: engage engineering director and customer-success if customer-facing impact

Post-incident checklist:
- Confirm customer impact and notify customer-success.
- Runbook review: update steps where delays occurred.
- Capacity & cost review for adjustments.

7) Appendix: examples and checklists
Example terraform snippet (gpu-cluster module use):
``
module \"gpu-cluster\" {
  source = \"git::ssh://git@repo/internal-terraform.git//modules/gpu-cluster?ref=v1.4.2\"
  name   = \"prod-gpu-usw2\"
  instance_type = \"p4d.24xlarge\"
  desired_capacity = 100
  max_capacity = 200
  tags = {
    team = \"infra\"
    project = \"redwood-inference\"
    env = \"prod\"
    owner = \"infra-gpu-capacity\"
  }
}
```
Pre-merge CI checklist (PR template):
- [ ] terraform fmt & tflint passed
- [ ] terraform validate & unit tests passed
- [ ] conftest/OPA policy checks passed
- [ ] reviewer (infra-sre + capacity owner) assigned
- [ ] estimated cost delta attached

Runbook handover template (minimal):
- Incident summary, timeline, mitigation steps taken, metrics dashboards, owners for follow-up (actions, owner, due date).

Operational metrics to monitor (dashboards):
- Fleet capacity utilization (avg & p95) per pool
- Queue length & mean wait time
- Provisioning time for new nodes (median + p95)
- Error rate by model & route
- Egress cost and network egress anomalies

Document maintenance and review cadence:
- Owner (infra-gpu-capacity) must review this playbook quarterly and after any P0/P1 incident.
- Major IaC or networking architecture changes require updating the playbook before rollout.

Related resources:
- /confluence/eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/infra-iac-and-gpu-fleet-guide-2026.json
- /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-capacity-and-infra-runbook-2026.json

If you have proposed changes to CI/CD gating or module behavior, open an RFC in the infra-team repo and tag reviewers from infra-sre, platform, and security.
